questions.question: A school minibus costs R360 000 and depreciates at 12% per annum. Calculate its value after 5 years under straight-line depreciation and under reducing-balance depreciation, and explain the structural difference between the two models, including their long-run behaviour.
questions.expected_answer: Straight-line uses A = P(1 − in): in = 0,12 × 5 = 0,6, so A = 360 000 × 0,4 = R144 000. The same fixed slice — 12% of the original R360 000, which is R43 200 — is removed every year. Reducing balance uses A = P(1 − i)ⁿ: A = 360 000 × 0,88⁵ = 360 000 × 0,52773 ≈ R189 983,49. Here each year removes 12% of the CURRENT value, so the rand amount lost shrinks annually — R43 200 in year one but only about R25 900 in year five — which is why reducing balance leaves roughly R46 000 more book value at the same rate. Long-run behaviour differs structurally: the straight line reaches zero after 1 ÷ 0,12 = 8⅓ years, while reducing balance multiplies by 0,88 each year and therefore shrinks forever without ever reaching zero.

questions.question: R15 000 is invested for 3 years at 8% per annum compounded quarterly. Calculate the accumulated amount, compare it with annual compounding at the same nominal rate, and explain why more frequent compounding pays more.
questions.expected_answer: Convert to the compounding clock first: the quarterly rate is 0,08 ÷ 4 = 0,02 and the number of periods is 3 × 4 = 12. Then A = 15 000 × 1,02¹² = 15 000 × 1,26824 ≈ R19 023,63. At 8% compounded annually, A = 15 000 × 1,08³ = 15 000 × 1,259712 = R18 895,68, so quarterly compounding pays about R128 more over the three years. The reason is timing: each quarter's interest joins the principal immediately and begins earning interest itself — March's interest is at work from April — instead of waiting for year-end. Interest earning interest sooner is the essence of compounding, so at the same quoted rate more frequent compounding always accumulates more, though each extra step of frequency adds less than the previous one. The non-negotiable discipline is a single clock: the rate per period and the number of periods must both refer to the same compounding period.

questions.question: Define nominal and effective interest rates, derive the effective rate of 8% per annum compounded quarterly, and use effective rates to decide between Bank X at 8,3% compounded annually and Bank Y at 8,1% compounded monthly.
questions.expected_answer: The nominal rate is the advertised annual headline, meaningless without its compounding frequency; the effective rate is the single once-a-year rate that would produce identical growth — what money actually grows by in one year. The link is 1 + i_eff = (1 + i_nom/m)^m. For 8% compounded quarterly: one rand becomes 1,02⁴ = 1,08243 in a year, so the effective rate is about 8,24% — above the nominal, as it must be whenever compounding happens more than once a year. For the contest: Bank X compounds annually, so its effective rate equals its nominal 8,3%. Bank Y: 1 + 0,081/12 = 1,00675, and 1,00675¹² = 1,08408, an effective rate of about 8,41%. Since 8,41% exceeds 8,3%, Bank Y is the better investment despite the smaller headline — twelve compounding paydays a year more than close the gap. The conclusion must be the comparison sentence quoting both effective rates, because nominal headlines with different frequencies can never be compared directly.
